content:
I recently noticed that Apple seems to have given up on Cinematic Mode, and a video experiment perfectly illustrates my disappointment with this.

The reason isn't that the feature is bad, but rather that it's so close to being truly usable that it makes it even harder to understand why Apple hasn't taken better advantage of the massive performance improvements between its iPhone 13 debut and the latest iPhone. Let me show you...

I've previously explained why I understand Apple not prioritizing updates to this feature, but at the same time I think Apple should update it so it can encourage future video creators and filmmakers—especially young people who may not have access to other filming equipment.

I have a friend who enjoys using a smartphone to approach strangers on the street and often gets them to say unexpected things. I decided to flip the situation, have him sit on a bench, and then use a smartphone—my iPhone 16 Pro Max—to film him.

I wanted to see how complex a scene Cinematic Mode could handle: a person sitting in the foreground, railings about 25 feet behind, and across a river, possibly close to a thousand feet further, the O2 Arena. Also, because he was sitting on a bench, his range of movement would be very limited.

The answer is... very close, but not quite. The overall effect is decent, but there's a noticeable halo issue between his legs and the railings, and when his head moves past the O2's support structures, those structures sometimes become sharp. When he spreads his arms, the river behind him also sometimes suddenly becomes sharp:

To be fair, CK thinks the average viewer watching this footage probably wouldn't notice the issue. If they're not a filmmaker or tech enthusiast who's familiar with how this feature works, they might not notice these flaws at all—and even if they did, they wouldn't find them bothersome. I suppose he might be right.

But this issue really bothers me, and I think even amateur filmmaking enthusiasts would share the same disappointment—and these people are precisely the target audience for this feature.

As I said at the beginning, my disappointment isn't because the feature is bad, but because I genuinely believe that if Apple properly leveraged the processing power and neural network capabilities of current iPhone chips, this feature could be dramatically improved. In fact, I'd expect a well-updated Cinematic Mode to handle scenes far more complex than this.

Do you agree with me? Do you want Apple to take Cinematic Mode seriously? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
